ch6_ex4_q1a: Picture a Rubik's cube: 3 layers, each a $3 \times 3$ square of 9 small cubes, so $3 \times 9 = 27$ unit cubes.
ch6_ex4_q1b: Estimate: $4^3 = 64$ and $4.5^3 \approx 91$, so $74.088$ sitting between them makes sense.
Calculator: use the $x^3$ key, or type $4.2$^$3$.
ch6_ex4_q1c: Pair the numbers that make a round result: $20 \times 15 = 300$, then $300 \times 12 = 3600$.
ch6_ex4_q2a: Think of the solid as a stack of identical thin slices, like a pile of coins. Volume = area of one slice $\times$ the stack height, whatever the slice's shape.
ch6_ex4_q2b: Unit check: $\text{cm}^2 \times \text{cm} = \text{cm}^3$. If your units don't come out cubed, a dimension is missing or doubled.
ch6_ex4_q3a: Exact first: $\pi \times 144 \times 14 = 2016\pi$. Estimate: $3 \times 2000 = 6000$, a bit under $6333.5$.
ch6_ex4_q3c: A right-angled triangular prism is half of a box: the $8 \times 7 \times 10$ box is $560$, so the prism is $280$.
ch6_ex4_q4b: Estimate: $35^\circ$ is about $\frac{1}{10}$ of a full turn. The full cylinder is $\pi \times 6.5^2 \times 7.1 \approx 942$, so the wedge should be roughly 94; the answer 91.6 fits.
ch6_ex4_q4c: Find the whole cylinder ($\pi \times 22.5^2 \times 18 \approx 28\,628$), then take $\frac{3}{4}$ of it.
ch6_ex4_q5a: A sphere fills about $52\%$ ($\frac{\pi}{6}$) of the cube that just encloses it: $2.4^3 \approx 13.8$ and $0.52 \times 13.8 \approx 7.2$.
Memory aid: Volume uses $r^3$ (cm$^3$); Surface uses $r^2$ (cm$^2$). The power matches the unit.
ch6_ex4_q5d: Make it meaningful: $523\,598.8\text{ cm}^3 \approx 0.52\text{ m}^3$, or about 524 L, since $1000\text{ cm}^3 = 1$ L.
ch6_ex4_q6d: Nice link: $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^3$ is also the volume of a cone with radius $r$ and height $r$. A quarter-sphere holds exactly as much as that cone.
ch6_ex4_q7a: Find the cylinder first ($\pi \times 36 \times 10 = 360\pi$), then take a third: $120\pi \approx 377.0$.
Why one third? If you fill a cone with water and pour it into a cylinder with the same base and height, it takes exactly three cones to fill it.
ch6_ex4_q7b: Lying on its side doesn't change anything: the 'height' is always measured from the base circle to the tip, at right angles to the base.
ch6_ex4_q8a: Why $\frac{1}{3}$: a cube can be cut into exactly 3 identical square pyramids, each using one face as its base and the same opposite corner as its apex.
ch6_ex4_q9a: Alternative: think of the block as the full $20 \times 10 \times 10$ box ($2000$) minus the missing $12 \times 5 \times 10$ chunk ($600$): $1400\text{ cm}^3$.
ch6_ex4_q9b: Exact form: $(240 + 18\pi) \times 35 = 8400 + 630\pi$. Then a single calculator step gives $10\,379.20$.
ch6_ex4_q10a: Sense check: the pyramid's height ($\approx 4.77$) must be less than the 5 cm slant height, because the slant height is the hypotenuse.
Since $\frac{1}{3} \times 3^2 = 3$, the pyramid's volume is just $3H$.
ch6_ex4_q10b: A cone is like a cylinder one third as tall: the solid acts like a cylinder of length $3 + \frac{2.5}{3} \approx 3.83$, so $V \approx 4\pi \times 3.83 \approx 48.17$.
ch6_ex4_q11a: Neat link: a hemisphere has the same volume as a cone of the same radius with height $2r$. So the whole solid is like one cone of height $2(3.5) + 10 = 17$: $\frac{1}{3}\pi \times 3.5^2 \times 17 \approx 218.08$.
ch6_ex4_q12a: Picture it: tripling the edges gives a $3 \times 3 \times 3$ arrangement of copies of the original cube, which is 27 copies.
ch6_ex4_q12b: Picture it: 8 small cubes (2 by 2 by 2) fit together to make the original cube, so each small one is $\frac{1}{8}$.
ch6_ex4_q12d: Factor: $2^2 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$. A wider, flatter cylinder can hold exactly the same amount.
ch6_ex4_q12e: Test with a $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cube: the new prism is $2 \times 0.5 \times 3 = 3$, three times the original.
ch6_ex4_q13: Conversion picture: 1 L is a $10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}$ cube, so divide $\text{cm}^3$ by 1000 to get litres.
ch6_ex4_q14a: The true value is $\frac{4}{3}\pi \times 64 \approx 268$, so using $\pi \approx 3$ underestimates by about $4.5\%$ (since $3$ is $4.5\%$ less than $\pi$).
ch6_ex4_q14b: Each ball sits in its own $8 \times 8 \times 8$ cube of space and fills only about $52\%$ ($\frac{\pi}{6}$) of it, which is why so much of a box of balls is air.
ch6_ex4_q14c: Rounding $32$ to $30$ makes the multiplication easy ($40 \times 30 \times 10$) but loses $800\text{ cm}^3$; that will matter in part f.
ch6_ex4_q14d: So in this estimate, the balls take up less than half of the box.
ch6_ex4_q14e: Type it in one go: $40 \times 32 \times 10 - 20 \times \frac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 4^3$, so no rounding happens in the middle.
ch6_ex4_q14f: Track the errors: the box estimate was $800$ too small and the balls estimate $20 \times 12.08 \approx 241.65$ too small, so the unfilled estimate is low by $800 - 241.65 = 558.35$.
ch6_ex4_q15: Why $\times 1000$: a $1\text{ m}$ cube holds $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ one-litre cubes (each $10\text{ cm}$ on a side).
ch6_ex4_q16: Write the total as one calculator line: $15\,000 - \left(160 + \frac{4}{3}\pi \times 8.5^3 + \frac{1}{3}\pi \times 14^2 \times 10\right)$.
Sense check: the packing (about $10\,215$) is roughly two thirds of the box, which fits three fairly small objects.
ch6_ex4_q17a: Similar triangles: $\frac{H - 3}{H} = \frac{4}{8}$, so the bottom is halfway to the apex and $H = 6$.
ch6_ex4_q17b: Check with the frustum formula $\frac{1}{3}h(X^2 + Xx + x^2) = \frac{1}{3} \times 3 \times (64 + 32 + 16) = 112$.
The removed tip is a half-size copy, so its volume is $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$ of the big pyramid: $\frac{1}{8} \times 128 = 16$.
ch6_ex4_q17c: $112 \div 6 \approx 18.7$; 18 bins only hold $108\text{ m}^3$, so 19 are needed.
ch6_ex4_q17d: Shortcut: $\text{m}^3 \to$ L is $\times 1000$, so $112\text{ m}^3 = 112\,000$ L. Equivalently, $1\text{ m}^3$ of water is 1 tonne.
ch6_ex4_q17e: Use volume scaling: a pyramid's volume is proportional to (height from apex)$^3$. Water plus tip is $\frac{72}{128}$ of the full pyramid, so $y = 6 \times \sqrt[3]{0.5625} \approx 4.95$.
Sense check: the answer must be more than half of 3 m (1.5 m) because the bottom half of the pool is narrower.
ch6_ex4_q18ai: Rearranged: $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3V}{4\pi}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{300}{\pi}}$. Since $4.5^3 \approx 91$ and $\frac{300}{\pi} \approx 95.5$, $r$ is just over 4.5.
ch6_ex4_q18aii: Shortcut for a sphere: $\text{SA} = \frac{3V}{r}$ (because $4\pi r^2 = 3 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \div r$). So $\frac{1200}{4.5708} \approx 262.5$.
ch6_ex4_q18bi: Check: $\pi \times 9 \times 14.15 \approx 400$. Substituting your answer back is the quickest way to catch a slip.
ch6_ex4_q18bii: Since $V = \pi r^2 h$, the curved surface $2\pi r h = \frac{2V}{r} = \frac{800}{3} \approx 266.67$ exactly, without using the rounded height.
ch6_ex4_q18cii: For a tall, thin pyramid the slant height is barely more than the vertical height ($33.47$ vs $33.33$), because half the base (3 cm) is tiny in comparison.
ch6_ex4_q18d: The best cylinder has height equal to its diameter: for 400 mL that is $r \approx 3.99$ cm with $\text{SA} = 6\pi r^2 \approx 300.5\text{ cm}^2$, close to the sphere but easy to stand up and stack.
ch6_ex4_q19a: Check by substituting back: $\pi r^2 \times \frac{V}{\pi r^2} = V$.
ch6_ex4_q19bii: Link to part (i): the radius doubled, so $h$ is a quarter: $31.83 \div 4 \approx 7.96 \approx 8.0$. Exactly, $h = \frac{25}{\pi}$.
ch6_ex4_q19c: Undo in reverse order: $V$ was made by squaring $r$, then multiplying by $\pi h$. So divide by $\pi h$ first, then square root.
ch6_ex4_q19d: For a real cylinder, $r$ must actually be greater than 0, and this needs $V > 0$ and $h > 0$ so the fraction under the root is positive.
ch6_ex4_q19eii: Scaling: the height is 1.5 times bigger, so the radius shrinks by $\sqrt{1.5} \approx 1.22$: $7.57 \div 1.22 \approx 6.2$.
ch6_ex4_q20: Surprise: the 1000 small balls have 10 times the total surface area of the big ball, because area only scales by $10^2 = 100$ while volume scales by $10^3$.
ch6_ex4_q21c: Tank (a) needs about 13 times as much material as tank (b) for the same 2000 L. Extreme shapes (very flat or very thin) waste material.
Units: $1\text{ m}^2 = 10\,000\text{ cm}^2$, so convert lengths to metres first rather than dividing an area by 100.
ch6_ex4_q22a: Test the formula: if $y = x$ it gives $\frac{1}{3}h \times 3x^2 = hx^2$ (a prism), and if $y = 0$ it gives $\frac{1}{3}hx^2$ (a pyramid). Both make sense.
ch6_ex4_q22b: The small pyramid is a $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$ scale copy of the full one, so its volume is $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{8}{27}$ of 180: $\frac{8}{27} \times 180 \approx 53.33$.
ch6_ex4_q23: Handy fact: 1 mm of rain on $1\text{ m}^2$ of roof is exactly 1 litre. So the tanks' $30\,925$ L divided by $170\text{ m}^2$ gives about 182 mm.
ch6_ex4_q24: With $h = 2r$: volumes $2\pi r^3$ vs $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, areas $6\pi r^2$ vs $4\pi r^2$. Both ratios are $\frac{3}{2}$.
Bonus: the sphere's area $4\pi r^2$ equals the cylinder's curved side exactly ($2\pi r \times 2r$).
ch6_ex4_q25: Shortcut for a muffin cup: the frustum formula works for cones too: $\frac{1}{3}\pi h(R^2 + Rr + r^2) = \frac{1}{3}\pi \times 4 \times (16 + 8 + 4) = \frac{112\pi}{3}$.
Exact comparison: the mixture is $500\pi \approx 1571$, more than the tin's $1500$, so the tin overflows slightly.
ch6_ex4_q26: Check $x = 0.3$ directly: the base is $1.4 \times 1.4$ and the height 0.3, so $V = 1.96 \times 0.3 = 0.588\text{ m}^3$.
The two answers sit either side of $x = \frac{1}{3}$ m, where the volume is largest: $\frac{16}{27}\text{ m}^3 \approx 593$ L. For any square sheet, the best cut is $\frac{1}{6}$ of the side.
ch6_ex4_q27: Doubling a volume does not double the radius: if there were no entrance, $R = 1.5 \times \sqrt[3]{2} \approx 1.89$ m. The answer is a bit more because the entrance doesn't grow.
Keep $\pi$ as a common factor throughout; it cancels when you solve for $R^3$.
ch6_ex4_q28a: Stacked balls touch top to bottom, so the height is (number of balls) $\times$ (diameter): $6 \times 2R$.
ch6_ex4_q28b: Keep it in terms of $R$; no calculator is needed because $\pi$ and $R$ stay as symbols.
ch6_ex4_q28c: Write $\pi R^2 \times 12R$ and collect powers: $R^2 \times R = R^3$.
ch6_ex4_q28d: This is Archimedes' result in disguise: each ball fills $\frac{2}{3}$ of its own slice of cylinder (radius $R$, height $2R$), so any number of stacked balls gives $2 : 3$.
ch6_ex4_q29a: Base area is $X^2$, so this is just $\frac{1}{3} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.
ch6_ex4_q29b: Label a diagram: $H$ is the whole height, $h$ is the frustum part, so the small top pyramid is the leftover $H - h$.
ch6_ex4_q29c: From $\frac{H - h}{H} = \frac{x}{X}$, cross-multiply to $XH - Xh = xH$, so $H(X - x) = Xh$.
Check: if $x = 0$ (no top cut off), the formula gives $H = h$, as it should.
ch6_ex4_q29d: Memorise the difference of cubes: $a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$. It is the source of the middle $Xx$ term in the frustum formula.
ch6_ex4_q30: Bar model: $\frac{5}{8} - \frac{2}{8} = \frac{3}{8}$ of the container is 27 scoops, so $\frac{1}{8}$ is 9 scoops. A quarter is $\frac{2}{8}$, so 18 scoops are left.
Check: a full container holds $8 \times 9 = 72$ scoops, and $\frac{5}{8} \times 72 = 45 = 27 + 18$.
